assessment.nobel_worthiness: A cubic-kilometre detector in Antarctic ice that opened a genuinely new observational window: high-energy neutrino astronomy. It is a detector-driven discovery of the kind I know well, with decades of patient calibration and background rejection behind it, and it ties astroparticle physics to cosmic-ray origins.
assessment.attribution: Halzen drove the concept and the collaboration, and Karle and Spiering are credited for leading the construction, instrumentation and the early analyses. A three-person prize is defensible, though IceCube is a large collaboration and AMANDA-era founders and other leaders could be argued for. I rely on the supplied credit and my own recollection of the history, which I have not checked.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The diffuse astrophysical flux was seen in 2013 and has been confirmed in several independent channels. The TXS 0506+056 association followed in 2017-18, then NGC 1068 and the Galactic-plane neutrino emission. Independent confirmation by other experiments is still thinner, since KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD are younger. The interpretation is stable.
uncertainties: Exact fair allocation of credit among the founders and the construction leaders.
The identification of individual source classes is still developing, so the discovery is the flux and the technique rather than a complete source picture.
Independent experimental confirmation is limited to date.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ground-based imaging atmospheric Cherenkov astronomy made the TeV sky observable and revealed supernova remnants, pulsar wind nebulae, active galaxies and the Galactic centre in very-high-energy gamma rays. The technique is clever and instrument-led, and it has produced a lasting, large catalogue.
assessment.attribution: Hofmann led H.E.S.S. and Aharonian is a leading theorist and early observer, with the HEGRA and H.E.S.S. results. The technique's pioneers, such as Weekes and the Whipple Crab detection, are not in the credited names, so the pair may not represent the decisive early contributions. That makes the credit uneven.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with several independent arrays (H.E.S.S., MAGIC, VERITAS) agreeing for about two decades and a successor, CTAO, under construction. Recognition is not premature.
uncertainties: Whether the technique's founders, outside the credited names, should share in or replace this configuration.
A discovery spread over many sources and many instruments is hard to pin to two people.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks are a precision-measurement invention, using the magic-wavelength trap to reach fractional uncertainties of order 1e-18. They have a direct impact on redefining the second, on tests of fundamental constants and on relativistic geodesy. The idea is original and the realisation is clear.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and Ye led the demonstrations of record accuracy and stability. The pair is a natural and compact configuration. Other groups (e.g. Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow) contributed to the work, but I see the two as decisive.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with many independent clocks worldwide. The redefinition of the second is under discussion but has not happened, so impact is still growing. Hall and Hänsch's 2005 prize covered the comb, which is a separate invention.
uncertainties: Atomic clocks and optical frequency standards are outside my core expertise, so I would defer to colleagues on the clock priority history.
Overlap with earlier trapped-ion clock work, already recognised in 2012 for Wineland, could complicate the framing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of the Higgs boson is arguably the most significant experimental result in particle physics of this century. It was a spectacular detector and collaboration achievement, with ATLAS and CMS built over two decades. The theory was recognised in 2013, but the experiments were not.
assessment.attribution: The credit problem is severe. The discovery was made by thousands of people, and the four credited names are the leaders of ATLAS and CMS at different stages. Jenni and Della Negra are the founding spokespersons or conceivers of ATLAS and CMS, Virdee also led CMS, and Gianotti was ATLAS spokesperson at the time of the 2012 announcement. Choosing three of four is a somewhat arbitrary cut, and the Prize rules do not allow a collaboration to be named.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature. The result is independently confirmed by two experiments and by LHC Run 2 coupling measurements. Recognition is overdue rather than premature.
uncertainties: No clean three-person attribution for a collaboration of this size, and my choice among the four named leaders is a judgement, not a verified finding.
The committee has historically been reluctant to honour large-collaboration leaders, which weakens the realistic prospects.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Correction of spherical aberration in electron lenses pushed transmission and scanning transmission electron microscopes to sub-angstrom resolution, an instrumentation breakthrough that overcame the long-standing Scherzer limit and gave atomic-resolution imaging of materials. Its impact on materials physics is wide and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Rose supplied the theory and design, Haider and Urban built and demonstrated the first corrected TEM, and Krivanek (not on this list) did the corrected STEM work. The three credited names form a coherent set, but the omission of the STEM branch may be a problem for a fair prize.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The technique was demonstrated in the late 1990s, is commercially widespread and has been confirmed independently, including by the competing STEM approach. Electron microscopy has been recognised before (Ruska 1986, cryo-EM in chemistry 2017), so novelty of the subject is reduced.
uncertainties: Whether the physics prize or chemistry is the natural home for a microscopy invention.
Credit relative to the corrected STEM developers who are not among the names offered.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The first horizon-scale images of M87* and Sgr A* used a continent-sized Earth-sized VLBI array at 1.3 mm. As a measurement it required major advances in instrumentation, calibration, phase referencing and imaging. It gave direct strong-field evidence on black-hole shadows, and the result is visually iconic.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed the shadow imaging concept and Doeleman built and led the EHT collaboration, while Zensus led the European partner and the mm-VLBI infrastructure. The EHT team is very large, and the credited three do not clearly cover the algorithm and technology contributors.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature. M87* was imaged in 2019 and Sgr A* in 2022, with polarization and later epochs consistent. However, there is a single collaboration and the image reconstruction involves modelling choices. Independent confirmation from other arrays is not yet there, and the scientific interpretation of the spin and jet launching is still open.
uncertainties: No independent second experiment confirms the images.
The decisive contributions of individuals in a large collaboration, and whether the 2020 prize for black-hole theory and the Galactic-centre orbits has already covered this area.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed-light injection reduces quantum noise in gravitational-wave interferometers. It was proposed by Caves in 1981 and realised in GEO600 and LIGO, where it increases the detection rate. It connects quantum optics and precision instrumentation, and it is a clear and original contribution that is now operational.
assessment.attribution: Caves provided the theoretical proposal, Schnabel led the GEO600 implementation and Mavalvala helped bring it to LIGO, while Kimble and others did the earlier squeezing experiments. The four-name list is too many for three seats, and other pioneers (Slusher, Walls, McKenzie, Lam) can be argued for.
assessment.maturity: Mature in application. It has been used in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600 since 2010-2019. The fundamental squeezing physics is older, and LIGO's detection was recognised in 2017, which makes this a subsidiary enabling technology.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would see it as a technique supporting an already-recognised discovery.
Complicated priority history between theory, early squeezing experiments and the interferometer application.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background from pulsar timing arrays, with the Hellings-Downs angular correlation, opens a new band of gravitational waves and probably reflects the supermassive black-hole binary population. This is a beautiful, long-baseline timing measurement and I find the instrumental case compelling.
assessment.attribution: The credit is spread across NANOGrav, EPTA, PPTA, CPTA and the IPTA, and the named people are leaders of different collaborations. Kramer and Hobbs led the EPTA and PPTA, Siemens was a NANOGrav founder, and McLaughlin is a NANOGrav co-founder. Any three is a hard choice and the pulsar-timing pioneers (Detweiler, Foster and Backer) are also relevant.
assessment.maturity: Not yet fully mature. The 2023 results show about 3-4 sigma evidence for the correlation, not an unambiguous detection, and the source of the signal (supermassive black-hole binaries or new physics) is not settled. Combined IPTA analyses are still in progress, so I would see it as somewhat premature for now.
uncertainties: Significance is below the usual discovery threshold and the signal origin is unresolved.
Four named people from several collaborations makes a three-person prize hard.
Whether the field would be better recognised after a confirmed detection.
